real_s1.explanation: The unit is most active on vehicles (cars, vans, buses, trucks, emergency vehicles) and on shorebirds/wading birds. Within those classes it responds most clearly to a sharp, in-focus main subject. The sharp-versus-slightly-blurry difference was strong in both the original photos and the new ones, and similar units did not share it. The unit is also weaker when there is no single clear subject. The right-versus-no-clear-direction contrast stayed high (95th percentile on new photos), but it mostly reflects that same subject-versus-no-subject effect. The apparent preference for right-facing over left-facing subjects reversed on new photos, so it is not reliable. The preference for medium-sized framing also weakened (84th percentile). Level-versus-tilted was unusual only in the original set, and similar units shared it.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds to vehicles such as vans, buses, emergency trucks and cars, and to wading birds. Within those classes it is most active when the photo has one clear, sharply focused main subject that takes up a moderate share of the frame, roughly a quarter to three quarters. It is weaker on slightly blurry subjects and on photos with no single main subject. The apparent preference for rightward over leftward facing reversed on new photos, so it is not a real property. The higher response to a facing subject than to one with no clear direction is mostly the general 'clear main subject' effect, and it was only borderline on new photos.

real_s3.explanation: The unit is most active on vehicles (cars, vans, trucks, buses) and on wading birds. Within those classes, the most reliable within-class effect is sharpness. It responds more to a sharp, in-focus main subject than to a slightly blurry one. This held strongly on new photos (99th percentile) and is not shared by the similar units. A preference for a clear single subject that has some facing direction, over photos with no main subject, replicated only at the threshold and is partly shared by similar units. The apparent right-over-left facing preference reversed on new photos. The moderate-frame-size preference also weakened below the threshold. Neither is reliable.

null_s1.explanation: The unit is most active on road vehicles (beach wagons, ambulances, fire engines, police vans, minibuses, trucks, cabs) and on shorebirds and waders (redshank, dowitcher, sandpiper, turnstone, oystercatcher, black stork). That is, on elongated subjects usually photographed from the side. Within those classes, none of the photo properties tested reliably shifts its activity. The picked rows on facing right, sharpness and medium framing all failed on new photos, and medium framing even reversed sharply (percentile 3). The other high-percentile rows look weak too: row 23 (level vs tilted) is shared with a similar unit at 97, and row 11 rests on the same subject-size story that just reversed. So what is particular to this unit is best described by its preferred classes, not by viewpoint, framing, lighting, tint or sharpness.

null_s2.explanation: The unit is most active on vehicles (cars, vans, buses, trucks) and on wading or shore birds, which are its top classes. None of the photo properties in the table reliably explains its activity within those classes. All four rows picked as specific to it (facing right, sharp over slightly blurry, a medium-sized subject over no single subject) failed on new photos, with d near zero or reversed. The other high rows either reflect traits its similar units share (level over tilted lines) or rest on small groups that come close to the failed size row (row 7). So it is best described by its class preference rather than by facing direction, framing, sharpness or lighting.

null_s3.explanation: The unit is most active on road vehicles (cars, vans, buses, trucks, emergency vehicles) and wading or shore birds, plus a few related classes. None of the photo properties in the questions reliably explains its activity within those classes. Every row picked as particular to it (right-facing subjects, sharp subjects, a subject filling a quarter to three quarters of the frame) failed on 129 new photos, and the frame-share effect reversed strongly. The other unusual rows, such as level horizons and the gaps against photos with no single main subject, rest on small groups of 11 to 14 photos and were not tested, so they cannot be trusted either. What the unit responds to is best described by its photo classes, not by viewpoint, framing, sharpness or lighting.
